summary: Describes changes to the sockets API needed to support IPv6, including a new socket address structure, address conversion functions and some new socket options. It aims to keep applications as portable with IPv6 as they were with IPv4. It obsoletes RFC 2133 and was replaced by RFC 3493.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how the sockets API, the library programs use to open connections and send datagrams, was changed so it can carry 128-bit IPv6 addresses. Existing programs keep working, and one program can talk to both IPv4 and IPv6 hosts without knowing which is which.

questions: basic socket interface extensions for ipv6

subtitle: The changes to the Berkeley sockets API that let ordinary TCP and UDP programs use 128-bit IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The sockets API makes the size of an IP address visible to applications, and IPv4 addresses are 32 bits while IPv6 addresses are 128. Programs written against the old API also had to keep working.
tldr.mechanism: A new address structure, sockaddr_in6, carries the IPv6 address, port, traffic class, flow label and scope. A new address family AF_INET6 selects it, new functions look up names and convert addresses for both families, and IPv4 destinations can be reached by writing them as IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2553 was Informational. It obsoleted RFC 2133 and has been obsoleted by RFC 3493, with RFC 3152 updating it.

sections.title: Why the Socket API Had to Change
sections.content:
The RFC opens with the size problem. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, while IPv6 interfaces are identified by 128-bit addresses. The socket interface makes the size of an IP address quite visible to an application, and virtually all TCP/IP applications for BSD-based systems have knowledge of the size of an IP address. Those parts of the API that expose the addresses must therefore be changed to accommodate the larger IPv6 address size.

IPv6 also introduces new features, such as the traffic class and the flow label, some of which must be made visible to applications via the API. The memo defines a set of extensions to the socket interface to support the larger address size and the new features of IPv6.

The memo is explicit that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind; it provides information for the Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: A program that opens a socket has to say where in memory to put an address, and the old structures are sized for 32-bit addresses. A bigger address needs a bigger structure.

sections.title: Design Considerations and What Must Change
sections.content:
Four requirements shaped the design. The API changes should provide both source and binary compatibility for programs written to the original API, so that existing program binaries continue to operate when run on a system supporting the new API, and existing applications that are re-compiled continue to operate. Simply put, the changes for IPv6 should not break existing programs. An additional mechanism for implementations to verify this is to check that the new symbols are protected by Feature Test Macros as described in IEEE Std 1003.1.

The changes should be as small as possible, to simplify the task of converting existing IPv4 applications to IPv6. Where possible, applications should be able to use this API to interoperate with both IPv6 and IPv4 hosts, and should not need to know which type of host they are communicating with. And IPv6 addresses carried in data structures should be 64-bit aligned, which is necessary to obtain optimum performance on 64-bit machine architectures.

The document then lists what has to change. The core socket functions, those dealing with setting up and tearing down TCP connections and sending and receiving UDP packets, were designed to be transport independent: where protocol addresses are passed as function arguments they are carried via opaque pointers. These functions need not change for IPv6, but a new IPv6-specific address data structure is needed.

The sockaddr_in structure is the protocol-specific data structure for IPv4. It actually includes 8 octets of unused space, and it is tempting to try to use this space to adapt it to IPv6. Unfortunately sockaddr_in is not large enough to hold the 16-octet IPv6 address as well as the other information, the address family and port number, that is needed, so a new address data structure must be defined.

IPv6 addresses are scoped, so they could be link-local, site, organization, global, or other scopes at this time undefined. To support applications that want to identify a set of interfaces for a specific scope, the new structure must have a field an implementation can use to identify that set of interfaces. The name-to-address translation functions gethostbyname() and gethostbyaddr() are left as they are and new functions are defined. The address conversion functions inet_ntoa() and inet_addr() are quite specific to 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so two analogous functions were designed that convert both families and carry an address type parameter. Finally, new interfaces are needed for the IPv6 traffic class, flow label and hop limit header fields, and new socket options to control the sending and receiving of IPv6 multicast packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The design had one overriding constraint: old programs must keep running unchanged. That is why almost everything new was added alongside the old, rather than replacing it.

sections.title: The IPv6 Address Structures
sections.content:
A new in6_addr structure holds a single IPv6 address and is defined by including <netinet/in.h>:

struct in6_addr { uint8_t s6_addr[16]; /* IPv6 address */ };

This data structure contains an array of sixteen 8-bit elements, which make up one 128-bit IPv6 address, and the address is stored in network byte order. The structure is usually implemented with an embedded union with extra fields that force the desired alignment level, in a manner similar to BSD implementations of struct in_addr.

The protocol-specific structure that carries IPv6 addresses is sockaddr_in6. For systems based on 4.3BSD it is:

struct sockaddr_in6 { sa_family_t sin6_family; /* AF_INET6 */ in_port_t sin6_port; /* transport layer port # */ uint32_t sin6_flowinfo; /* IPv6 traffic class & flow info */ struct in6_addr sin6_addr; /* IPv6 address */ uint32_t sin6_scope_id; /* set of interfaces for a scope */ };

The sin6_family field identifies this as a sockaddr_in6 structure and must be AF_INET6. The sin6_port field contains the 16-bit UDP or TCP port number, stored in network byte order. The sin6_flowinfo field is a 32-bit field containing two pieces of information, the traffic class and the flow label. The sin6_addr field holds one 128-bit IPv6 address, stored in network byte order. The sin6_scope_id field is a 32-bit integer that identifies a set of interfaces as appropriate for the scope of the address: for a link scope it would be an interface index, and for a site scope a site identifier, with the mapping left to the implementation and to future specifications on site identifiers.

The ordering of elements in the structure is specifically designed so that when the sin6_addr field is aligned on a 64-bit boundary, the start of the structure is also aligned on a 64-bit boundary, for optimum performance on 64-bit architectures.

The RFC warns that sockaddr_in6 will normally be larger than the generic sockaddr structure. On many existing implementations the size of struct sockaddr_in equals the size of struct sockaddr, with both being 16 bytes, and any existing code that makes that assumption needs to be examined carefully when converting to IPv6.

The 4.4BSD release made a small but incompatible change: the sa_family field of sockaddr changed from a 16-bit value to an 8-bit value, and the space saved was used to hold a length field named sa_len. The structure above cannot be correctly cast into the newer sockaddr, so an alternative is provided for systems based on 4.4BSD, adding a sin6_len field and an 8-bit family field, with all other fields identical. Systems providing that version must also declare SIN6_LEN, so applications can tell which variant they are built against.
sections.plainLanguage: Two structures replace one: a plain holder for the 16 address bytes, and a larger one that also carries the port, the traffic class and the flow label, plus which set of interfaces the address scope refers to.

sections.title: Using the Structures with the Socket Functions
sections.content:
Applications call socket() to create a socket descriptor that represents a communication endpoint, and the arguments tell the system which protocol to use and what format address structure will be used in later calls. To create an IPv4/TCP socket an application makes the call s = socket(PF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0), and to create an IPv4/UDP socket s = socket(PF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0). IPv6/TCP and IPv6/UDP sockets are created by using the constant PF_INET6 instead of PF_INET in the first argument.

Once the application has created a PF_INET6 socket, it must use the sockaddr_in6 address structure when passing addresses in to the system. The functions used to pass addresses into the system are bind(), connect(), sendmsg() and sendto(). The system uses the same structure to return addresses to applications that are using PF_INET6 sockets, and the functions that return an address from the system to an application are accept(), recvfrom(), recvmsg(), getpeername() and getsockname().

No changes to the syntax of the socket functions are needed to support IPv6, because all of the address-carrying functions use an opaque address pointer and carry an address length as a function argument.

Two further portability helpers are added. The sockaddr_storage structure is designed to be large enough and aligned enough to hold the address structure of any family, so portable code can declare one variable and use it for either IPv4 or IPv6. And the interface index functions map between interface names such as le0 and the small positive integers the kernel assigns to interfaces, starting at 1, with 0 never used, and may have gaps.
sections.plainLanguage: Creating an IPv6 socket means passing one different constant. Everything else about the calls stays the same, and the length of the address is passed alongside it so the system knows how many bytes to read.

sections.title: Reaching IPv4 Nodes from an IPv6 Application
sections.content:
The API provides two kinds of compatibility. The first is compatibility with existing applications: systems must provide complete source and binary compatibility with the original API, must continue to support PF_INET sockets and the sockaddr_in structure, and applications must be able to create IPv4/TCP and IPv4/UDP sockets using the PF_INET constant. Applications should be able to hold a combination of IPv4/TCP, IPv4/UDP, IPv6/TCP and IPv6/UDP sockets simultaneously within the same process, and applications using the original API should continue to interoperate with IPv4 nodes.

The second is compatibility between IPv6 applications and IPv4 applications. This uses the IPv4-mapped IPv6 address format defined in the IPv6 addressing architecture specification. The IPv4 address is encoded into the low-order 32 bits of the IPv6 address, and the high-order 96 bits hold the fixed prefix 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF. Such addresses are written as ::FFFF:<IPv4-address>, and can be generated automatically by the getipnodebyname() function when the specified host has only IPv4 addresses.

An application may use PF_INET6 sockets to open TCP connections to IPv4 nodes, or send UDP packets to IPv4 nodes, simply by encoding the destination's IPv4 address as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address and passing it, within a sockaddr_in6 structure, in the connect() or sendto() call. When an application uses PF_INET6 sockets to accept TCP connections from IPv4 nodes, or to receive UDP packets from IPv4 nodes, the system returns the peer's address in the accept(), recvfrom() or getpeername() call using a sockaddr_in6 structure encoded this way.

Few applications will likely need to know which type of node they are interoperating with, but for those that do, the IN6_IS_ADDR_V4MAPPED() macro is provided.
sections.plainLanguage: One program can talk to both kinds of host. To reach an IPv4 machine from an IPv6 socket, write the IPv4 address in the low half of an IPv6 address and leave the top half as the fixed prefix.

sections.title: The New Functions and Definitions
sections.content:
The library section adds functions for looking up names and converting addresses. getipnodebyname() takes a name, an address family, a flags value and a pointer for the error code, and must be thread safe; the flags select which address types are searched for and returned, with AI_DEFAULT defined as the combination of AI_V4MAPPED and AI_ADDRCONFIG. getipnodebyaddr() does the reverse lookup, also thread safe. getaddrinfo() is the protocol-independent lookup from the POSIX 1003.1g draft, and must also be thread safe; it returns a linked list of addrinfo structures that the caller frees with freeaddrinfo(). getnameinfo() converts an address and port back into text, and gai_strerror() turns an error code into a message.

For address conversion, inet_pton() converts an address from its standard text presentation form into its numeric binary form, and inet_ntop() does the reverse. For IPv6 addresses the buffer must be at least 46 octets, and for IPv4 addresses at least 16 octets, which is why the constants INET6_ADDRSTRLEN and INET_ADDRSTRLEN are defined. Two constants are defined to help applications size their buffers for the reverse lookup: NI_MAXHOST is 1025 and NI_MAXSERV is 32.

The summary of new definitions then lists, by header, everything the memo adds: IF_NAMESIZE and struct if_nameindex in <net/if.h>; the AI_ and EAI_ and NI_ constants and struct addrinfo in <netdb.h>; the IN6ADDR_ constants, INET6_ADDRSTRLEN, IPPROTO_IPV6, the IPV6_ socket options, SIN6_LEN, the in6addr_any and in6addr_loopback variables and the in6_addr, ipv6_mreq and sockaddr_in6 structures in <netinet/in.h>; and AF_INET6, PF_INET6 and struct sockaddr_storage in <sys/socket.h>.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also defines the lookup and conversion routines, so a program can ask for a name and get back either kind of address, and can print an address back out as text.
